title: High Selectivity Towards Formate Production by Electrochemical Reduction of Carbon Dioxide at Copper–Bismuth Dendrites
abstract: Fossil fuels have powered economic growth since the industrial revolution. However, this has caused severe environmental pollution, including increased concentration of CO2 in the atmosphere. The capture and electrochemical reduction (ERC) of CO2 released from power plant exhausts could provide a carbon-neutral path towards the production of chemical fuels. However, lack of selective, efficient, stable, and earth-abundant catalysts presents a major hurdle to the widespread deployment of ERC technology. Copper as films, nanoparticles, and nanostructures has been extensively tested as an ERC electrocatalyst. For example, Hori and later Kuhl et al. reported the synthesis of a variety of (C1 to C3) hydrocarbon products and alcohols. Larger molecules could also be produced by the application of a higher overvoltage. In contrast, CO and formate can be obtained by a simple 2 e reduction, which minimizes overvoltage and increases efficiency. Formate is a liquid at room temperature and pressure, and features a high hydrogen–storage capacity with low toxicity, which is desirable for application in alkaline fuel cells. Main-group metals including In, Sn, Tl, Pb, and Bi have been studied for high-selectivity electrocatalytic production of formate. Bi was first reported as a potential ERC catalyst for formate synthesis twenty years ago, displaying a faradaic efficiency (FE) of 77 %. Pb and Sn were also investigated for formic acid synthesis in a bicarbonate solution. However, the initial FE of 80 % was observed to deteriorate over time. A later study by Agarwal et al. also demonstrated a similar FE (80 %) with Sn-based electrodes. Recently, Zhang et al. prepared and tested SnOx nanoparticles in carbonate solutions which could achieve 90 % FE. A high formate selectivity ( 100 %) was demonstrated by Bocarsly and coworkers with anodized indium nanoparticles. However, reduced In particles displayed a significantly reduced FE for formate production. In a successive work, mechanistic studies performed with ATR-IR spectroelectrochemistry suggested that In and Sn could reduce CO2 via a surface-adsorbed carbonate. In contrast, Pb supports the formation of an oxide layer during CO2 reduction, whereas Bi produces a metastable oxide in which the performance is independent of oxide thickness. This suggests that CO2 reduction mechanisms in these materials might be different. Recently, nanoscale dendritic Bi electrodeposited on a carbon paper has shown a FE of 96 % with a current density of 15 mA cm 2 at 1.8 VSCE. Upon employing pulse electrodeposition to grow Bi nanoflakes, a high selectivity of 80 % towards formate production at 0.4 VRHE could be achieved. A simple approach to tailor the performance of an ERC catalyst to maximize selectivity towards formate consists in combining Cu, a versatile ERC catalyst, with a main-group element such as Bi. Incorporation of Bi is known to suppress the rate of H2 evolution reaction (HER). Therefore, it is expected that the combination of Cu and Bi could result in a high activity and selectivity for formate productions. The Cu–Bi catalyst could also benefit from bimetallic effects, in which the adsorption strength of reaction intermediates could be affected by the local surface atomic configuration. Bimetallic catalysts have been investigated for CO2 reduction. The electrochemical reduction of CO2 provides an alternative carbon-neutral path for renewable synthesis of fuels and valueadded chemicals. This work demonstrates that dendritic, bimetallic Cu–Bi electrocatalysts with nanometer-sized grains are capable of formate generation with a high selectivity. Optimizing composition of electrocatalyst could achieve a faradic efficiency of 90 % at 0.8 to 0.9 VRHE, and a partial current of more than 2 mA cm . The combination of Cu with Bi enables modulation of the adsorption strength of intermediates. This leads to an increased selectivity and suppressed formation of spurious species, especially hydrogen and CO. Comparison of product distribution for Cu–In versus Cu–Bi indicated that Bi is essential to induce a favorable adsorption configuration of the intermediate species and to promote formate production.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text:
Fossil fuels have powered economic growth since the industrial revolution. However, this has caused severe environmental pollution,[1] including increased concentration of CO2 in the atmosphere.[2] The capture and electrochemical reduction (ERC) of CO2 released from power plant exhausts could provide a carbon-neutral path towards the production of chemical fuels. However, lack of selective, efficient, stable, and earth-abundant catalysts presents a major hurdle to the widespread deployment of ERC technology. Copper as films, nanoparticles, and nanostructures[3–7] has been extensively tested as an ERC electrocatalyst. For example, Hori[8] and later Kuhl et al.[9] reported the synthesis of a variety of (C1 to C3) hydrocarbon products and alcohols. Larger molecules could also be produced by the application of a higher overvoltage. In contrast, CO and formate can be obtained by a simple 2 e reduction, which minimizes overvoltage and increases efficiency. Formate is a liquid at room temperature and pressure, and features a high hydrogen–storage capacity with low toxicity, which is desirable for application in alkaline fuel cells.[10] Main-group metals including In, Sn, Tl, Pb, and Bi have been studied for high-selectivity electrocatalytic production of formate.[11] Bi was first reported as a potential ERC catalyst for formate synthesis twenty years ago, displaying a faradaic efficiency (FE) of 77 %.[12] Pb and Sn were also investigated for formic acid synthesis in a bicarbonate solution. However, the initial FE of 80 % was observed to deteriorate over time.[13] A later study by Agarwal et al. also demonstrated a similar FE (80 %) with Sn-based electrodes.[14] Recently, Zhang et al. prepared and tested SnOx nanoparticles in carbonate solutions which could achieve 90 % FE.[15] A high formate selectivity ( 100 %) was demonstrated by Bocarsly and coworkers with anodized indium nanoparticles. However, reduced In particles displayed a significantly reduced FE for formate production.[16] In a successive work, mechanistic studies performed with ATR-IR spectroelectrochemistry suggested that In and Sn could reduce CO2 via a surface-adsorbed carbonate. In contrast, Pb supports the formation of an oxide layer during CO2 reduction, whereas Bi produces a metastable oxide in which the performance is independent of oxide thickness.[17] This suggests that CO2 reduction mechanisms in these materials might be different. Recently, nanoscale dendritic Bi electrodeposited on a carbon paper has shown a FE of 96 % with a current density of 15 mA cm 2 at 1.8 VSCE.[18] Upon employing pulse electrodeposition to grow Bi nanoflakes, a high selectivity of 80 % towards formate production at 0.4 VRHE could be achieved.[19]

Therefore, it is expected that the combination of Cu and Bi could result in a high activity and selectivity for formate productions. The Cu–Bi catalyst could also benefit from bimetallic effects, in which the adsorption strength of reaction intermediates could be affected by the local surface atomic configuration.[20] Bimetallic catalysts have been investigated for CO2 reduction. [22, 23] A wide range of Cu–In alloy compositions have been reported with up to 60 % FE towards formate production, whereas conditions for predominant generation of syngas (mixtures of CO and hydrogen) were also identified.[24] Au-Pd alloys was also found to be slightly better than pristine Au for CO production.[25] Au3Cu electrocatalysts displayed the highest activity among all monodisperse Au-Cu nanoparticles.[26]
With regard to reported efficiencies and production rates in CO2 electroreduction processes, in many cases these values are the result of experiments where few parameters are being explored. A recent study demonstrated that varying the transport rate to the electrode, cell pressure, and temperature all result in significant (up to 50 %) changes in the distribution, selectivity and production rates.[27] Consequently, most studies represent a spread of performance values over a range of parameters instead of precise and specific quantities.
Since Cu and Bi are mutually insoluble, they cannot form solid solutions and only mechanical mixtures are possible.[28] However, a metastable BiCu compound has been reported in context of superconductor materials.[29–31] In this work, the ECR of CO2 was studied with dendritic Cu–Bi electrocatalyst of different compositions (20–60 % Bi). These catalysts were found capable of converting CO2 into formate with a high selectivity (up to 90 %) at 0.8 VRHE.

sections.heading: Results and Discussion
sections.text:
Electrocatalyst materials: synthesis and structural characterization
Dendritic Cu, Bi, and bimetallic Cu–Bi structures were grown onto Cu substrates by electrodeposition, resulting in a continuous layer without pinholes. Dendrite formation requires that growth occur at the limiting diffusion current and the presence of anisotropy in the system. The anisotropic requirements can be fulfilled by either the crystal structure and/or by an anisotropic growth rate.[32] Since Cu has a cubic structure, incorporation of chloride in the electrolyte introduces anisotropy by creating a crystallographic direction-dependent rate of growth.[33] Cu dendrites were observed to have a regular tree-like morphology with side branches protruding at 608, with main and secondary branches displaying growth along the <110> directions (Figure 1 a).[33] Conversely, Bi possessing a rhombohedral structure provides anisotropy because of crystal asymmetry. This results in dendrites with a mixture of branched features (Figure 1 b), and irregular but well-developed parallel facets (inset in Figure 1 b).[34] The composition of Cu–Bi dendritic films was adjusted by varying the relative concentration of metal ions in the electroplating solutions (Figure 2). Modulation of metal ion concentrations for compositional control was found to be preferable to varying the applied potential. Since the standard redox potential of Cu2+ and Bi3+ are similar, varying the applied potential resulted in an approximately invariant composition.[35] The morphology and microstructure of the elemental and bimetallic dendrites could be easily reproduced. Because of the difference in crystal structure, crystal symmetry, and the lattice mismatch ( 16 %) between Cu and Bi,[31] it is expected that the Cu–Bi dendrites would consist of separate Cu and Bi grains growing onto each other without any epitaxial relationship. SEM images presented in Figure 3 confirm this hypothesis, as dense dendritic architectures with branches of roughly 100 nm protruding in different directions can be easily observed. Figure 3 a, b display the same dendrite cluster at different magnifications, whereas Figure 3 c contains a view of the film cross section. The dendritic film was observed to be approximately 8 mm in thickness with a continuous interfacial layer ( 120 nm) isolating the substrate from the electrolyte. The dense, submicron features of these dendrites strongly indicate a high surface area, which is advantageous for catalysis. The overall dendritic film thickness varied between 3 and 6 mm for different samples, with an average thickness of 4 mm. In Cu-

However, samples with Bi >50 at % were observed to collapse and fracture into dense aggregates (see the Supporting Information, Figure S5). Additionally, the ERC tests were not observed to modify the composition and morphology of the electrodes (Table S1 and Figure S5).
X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns of the catalyst samples with different compositions are provided in Figure 4. Pure Cu dendritic films (bottom) clearly display (111) and (2 0 0) reflections, whereas the XRD pattern for pure Bi (top) displays a large number of corresponding Bi reflections. Upon increasing Bi fraction, all the Cu–Bi alloys begin to display two wide and shallow peaks centered around 2q= 308 and 43.58. The first peak (308) corresponds to a planar spacing of about 0.3 nm, which is close to the d-spacing of the Bi (0 1 2) planes. This indicates a significant distortion of the Bi structure (the c axis of rhombohedral Bi has a lattice constant of 0.33 nm) and suggests a limited incorporation of Cu in the Bi phase. The second peak (43.58) corresponds to the Cu (111) plane, in which the broadening and shifting can be attributed to the small grain size and limited incorporation of Bi and/or internal stresses in
the Cu matrix. A third peak could be observed for catalysts with 20 at % Bi corresponding to Bi (1 2 2) plane. Dendritic films with a higher Bi fraction exhibit the two major peaks (308, 43.58) together with additional Bi peaks, in which their intensity is proportional to the overall Bi fraction. Four additional peaks corresponding to the metastable BiCu intermetallic phase are also present in the bimetallic samples. However, the intensity of these peaks is relatively independent of the composition, and the corresponding volume fraction of this phase is quite small. Overall, the results from XRD patterns of dendritic Cu–Bi suggest the formation of a mechanical mixture.
Grain size of the samples was estimated by performing Scherrer analysis on the XRD patterns. Scherrer analysis of the XRD data (Figure S6) indicates that the grain size of pure metals is approximately 25 nm, whereas the bimetallic alloys have an average grain size of 12–19 nm. A notable increase in the relative grain size was observed for the 60 at % Bi catalysts. HR-TEM imaging and SAED were also performed for selected Cu–Bi films to provide additional insight into the crystal structure, grain size, and phase distribution within the dendrites. Figure 5 a, b display the overall view and high-resolution image of a typical dendrite tip (20 at % Bi), respectively. The circled areas in the image highlight the single crystal regions, confirming a small grain size of 4–10 nm. This value is notably smaller than that obtained by Scherrer analysis. However, the acquired SAED pattern for the same area (Figure 5 c) is in good agreement with the data provided by XRD analysis. Data from TEM images confirmed that the grain size for different phases in the dendrites is much smaller than the estimates provided by either Scherrer method or SEM images. TEM images also helped to establish the presence of an intimate contact between Cu and Bi phases, which could facilitate the formation of a bimetallic interface. Additionally, the presence of a very thin (few nm) amorphous layer in the lower left region (Figure 5 b) also suggests the presence of an oxide phase.
XPS measurements were performed on a Cu–Bi electrode (Bi 80 at %) before and after the ERC test to analyze the change in surface composition/chemistry. Figure 6 shows the acquired HR XPS spectra for Cu, Bi and O atoms. The predominantly metallic behavior of pristine Cu is indicated by the presence of a strong Cu 2p peak at binding energy of approximately 933 eV. After immersion, evolution of a very shallow bump between 937 and 945 eV suggests the formation of a small quan-

Electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 : product distribution and electrochemical response
Figure 7 shows the product distribution obtained at pure Cu and Bi catalysts, as a function of applied potential. Dendritic Cu shows a high yield for H2 production at all potentials with greater than 70 % efficiency. Similarly, formate production is also independent of applied potential with a FE of roughly 9 %, whereas CO, methane, and ethylene are formed as minor products at or below 2 % FE. In contrast, formate production is significant over dendritic Bi, with approximately 1 % CO as a minor product. A maximum FE of 62 % for formate production was achieved at 0.9 V versus RHE, while at other potentials it averages above 45%. Notably, the FE for formate production over Bi electrodes in this study is significantly lower than those reported in the literature.[18, 19] Hence, it would be very interesting to compare the performance of pure Bi versus Cu–Bi electrodes in other laboratories.
The product distribution as a function of applied potential for the Cu–Bi electrocatalysts is summarized in Figure 8. The films with the lowest Bi content (20 at %, Figure 7 a) reported a high formate production (FE over 85 %) at 0.8 V versus RHE. Upon increasing the overpotential, FE for formate decreased but improved for HER by up to 30 %. The highest FE for formate production was achieved by using 40 at % Bi catalyst at 0.9 V (Figure 7 b). At this composition, the efficiency for formate and H2 production exhibit opposite trends. The FE efficiency for formate increases from 1.0 to 1.1 V, followed by a sharp decrease at the potential of 1.2 V (not shown).
A similar trend was observed for 60 at % Bi films with a maximum FE of 85 % at 0.8 V. Additionally, a small peak in CO production is seen at 0.9 V with CO efficiency reaching 8 %. Among the bimetallic catalysts, the lowest formate efficiency (45–50 %) was displayed by 80 at % Bi films, independent of reduction potential. This composition also displayed the highest tendency to form CO at lower potentials, with approximately 25 % efficiency. A balance between the HER and formate production could be observed over Cu–Bi electrocatalysts, with CO as the minor product. (except for 80 at % Bi). The FE for formate production is highest at the lowest reduction potentials ( 0.8 and 0.9 VRHE ; Figure S7). Upon plotting the FE of formate production against catalyst composition (Figure 9), 20 and 60 % Bi electrodes exhibit two maxima at 0.8 V. However, only a single maximum at 0.9 V is observed with 40 at % Bi film, highlighting an optimum balance in a postulated bimetallic mechanism. This indicates that synergistic effects between Cu and Bi may lead to more efficient formate production than with pure metals. Correspondingly, HER formation is reduced, reaching a minimum efficiency below 12 %.
The total and partial current densities were calculated by using the measured product distribution, current data from every ERC experiment, and the geometric area of the electrocatalysts. Geometric area was used given the difficulty in accurate measurement of true surface area by either electrochemical impedance spectroscopy or porosimetry. Although not ideal, this approximation is acceptable for a direct comparison of the different Cu–Bi electrocatalysts having a similar morphology and thickness. However, the significant difference in morphology of pure Cu and Bi dendrites vs. alloy dendrites would result in a systematic error when comparing pure metals to bimetallic catalysts.
The total and partial current densities for the three major products (H2, formate, and CO) are shown in Figure 10 a–d. Figure 10 a shows the total current density as a function of the catalyst. Pure dendritic Cu showed the highest overall current density, followed by dendritic Bi, and the current density was observed to be proportional to the Bi content in bimetallic catalysts. The high total current density in the (pure) dendritic Cu is primarily owed to extensive HER, as shown in Figure 10 d. Although the incorporation of Bi in Cu reduces the overall cur-

A synergistic effect between Cu and Bi suppresses the unwanted HER in favor of substantial formate production. The partial current densities in bimetallic

sections.heading: Reaction mechanism
sections.text:
Because of the intimate contact between Cu and Bi grains (Figure 5 b), it can be assumed that Cu–Bi catalysts operates as a bimetallic system. This assumption is supported by the higher FE of the bimetallic catalysts for formate production ( 90 % at 0.8 to 0.9 VRHE) compared with the pure metals Cu and Bi. The observed enhancement in formate production is partially correlated to the suppression of both HER and the CO formation rates over the Cu–Bi catalyst. Owing to the occurrence of similar chemical bonds, linear scaling relationships are commonly observed between the adsorption energy of the various CO2 reduction intermediates at a given metal substrate. [36] The

This could possibly contribute to the observed decrease in the minimum theoretical applied potential required for the product formation.[21] In our previous work, Cu–In alloys of various compositions achieved 30 % to 60 % formate genera-
tion with a significant CO (up to 40 %) production.[25] Upon comparing the above data, it can be concluded that the substitution of In with Bi leads to a stronger effective suppression of the HER and CO formation.
The reduction of CO2 to CO or formate is known to proceed through two distinct mechanisms. Proton coupled electron transfer (PCET) of the surface adsorbed CO2 leads to the formation of either carboxylic acid [*C(O)OH] or formate [*OC(O)H] , in which two different chemical functional groups are possible. Further reduction of [*C(O)OH] results in adsorbed CO, whereas the [*OC(O)H] binds to the O atom at the surface, making it impossible to form CO.[37] The formic acid reaction paths consists of the following two reactions [Equations (1) and (2)]:

The monodentate intermediate [*C(O)OH] can terminate as either formate or can proceed to CO, and potentially even further to yield higher hydrogenated products ; as observed with Cu–In catalysts[25] and pure Bi.
Therefore, preferential formate production is dependent on the relative adsorption strength (DGads) of the CO2 reduction intermediates at In versus Bi. Unfortunately, the adsorption strength of [*OC(O)H] is similar for most main-group elements of interest (Sn, Pb, Cd, In, Tl).[38] The similarity between electronegativity and electron affinity of In and Bi suggests that their (DGads) may also be similar. This prevents any attempt to qualitatively predict the outcome trend. Further insight into the occurrence of reaction path (1) + (2) versus the mechanism (3)–(5) could be attained by DFT methods.[39, 40]
Observing the product distribution trends as a function of applied potential and catalyst composition reveals that FE for formate decreases at more negative potentials, mainly because
of the concomitant increase in hydrogen formation. However, the 40 % Bi catalyst presents a different trend with a maximum formate FE at achieved at 0.9 V. This can be attributed to its smaller grain size (Figure S6). Catalytic activity and selectivity have been observed to increase with a smaller grain size. This observation is supported by two different effects of (1) changes in population of low-coordinated surface sites,[41] or (2) by a correlation between the catalytic activity and grain boundary density.[42] A similar mechanism may be responsible for the high FE in case of the 40 % Bi catalyst, in which a smaller grain size would induce a larger interface density and increased availability of active sites.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text:
We studied the electrochemical reduction of CO2 at dendritic Cu, Bi, and Cu–Bi alloys with varying compositions. The dendritic structures displayed a high density of defect sites because of the crystal lattice and symmetry mismatch. The high availability of these defects such as grain boundaries and twins could serve as active catalytic sites. Whereas the pure metals

exhibited selectivity for the activation of CO2 reduction (Cu) and formate production (Bi), the Cu–Bi dendrites exhibit a much lower current density for hydrogen/CO evolution reaction, and a much higher selectivity towards formate, up to about 90 % at 40–60 at % Bi and 0.8 to 0.9 VRHE. Notably, this work illustrated that the combination of a transition metal (Cu) with a main-group metal (Bi), exhibiting a close contact between the two constituents, can modulate the relative adsorption strength of the intermediates, thereby supporting formate generation. The relatively high purity of the obtained product is useful for the direct feed of a hydrogen fuel cell or for utilization as an industrial raw material.

sections.heading: Fabrication of electrocatalysts
sections.text:
Electrodeposition experiments were performed in a vertical threeelectrode cell and controlled by using a potentiostat (Biologic SP150). Immediately prior to electrodeposition, the substrates were rinsed with acetone and methanol, followed by a 1 min etch with H2SO4 (10 % v/v), and a final rinse with deionized water. The working electrode surface area was kept constant at 3 cm2 (1.5 cm 2 cm) for all experiments. A Pt-coated mesh was used as the counter electrode, whereas a mercurous sulfate electrode (MSE, EMSE = 0.650 VSHE) served as the reference. The counter electrode was immersed for 1 h in concentrated HNO3 (50 % v/v) before each experiment. Milli-Q water (resistivity 18.2 MW cm) was used for all experiments.
Pure Cu, Bi and bimetallic Cu–Bi films were all grown by electrodeposition. Dendritic Cu films were grown at a constant potential of 0.95 V versus MSE from an acidic solution of CuSO4 (10 mm ; Alfa Aesar, 99.99 %), H2SO4 (0.5 m; Sigma Aldrich, 98 %) and NaCl (0.5 m; Fischer Scientific, 99.99 %) on a Cu (100 nm)/Si substrate. The film was grown to a charge density of 1 C cm 2, corresponding to a nominal thickness of 650 nm. Dendritic Bi was deposited on a similar Cu/Si substrate at a potential of 0.85 V versus MSE to a charge density of 4 C cm 2 (nominal thickness 3.7 mm), by using an electrolyte containing Bi(NO3)3 (25 mm; Alfa Aesar, 99.99 %) and HNO3 (1.3 m; Sigma Aldrich, 70 %). [23]
Cu–Bi alloys were electrodeposited on Au (40 nm)/Si substrate by using an electrolyte containing HNO3 (0.5 m) and varying concentrations of Cu2O (Alfa Aesar, 99.99 %) and Bi(NO3)3 (Sigma Aldrich, 99.99 %). The composition of the electrolytes was adjusted such that the total metal ion concentration [Cu+] + [Bi3 +] remained constant (20 mm). Cu–Bi films were grown potentiostatically at 1.45 V versus MSE, by varying the relative concentration of [Cu2+] and [Bi3 +] to achieve the target compositions. Deposition was terminated at a charge density of 4 C cm 2, corresponding to an equivalent thickness of 4.6 mm.

sections.heading: Electrode characterization
sections.text:
The surface features of the catalysts were acquired by using scanning electron microscopy (FEI Quanta 650 SEM) in secondary–electron mode. An internally mounted energy dispersive X-ray (EDX) spectroscopy instrument, employing an acceleration voltage of 15 kV and a spot size of 4 nm> , was used to determine the film compositions.
XRD was utilized to identify the phase/crystallographic data of the catalyst films. Grazing incidence XRD (GI-XRD) measurements were performed by using a CuKa (l= 1.54 ) radiation source on a Philips PANalytical X’Pert Pro MPD (Multi-Purpose Diffractometer—Almelo, Netherlands) with an Eulerian–cradle stage. The 2q scans were conducted at a fixed omega angle of 18 with a step size of 0.058 and a dwell time of 1.4 s.
High-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HR-TEM, FEI Titan 300 kV) was used to gain further understanding of grain size, crystallography, and structure of the Cu–Bi electrocatalysts. Sample preparation was done by scraping Cu–Bi samples onto a carbon TEM grid. The HR-TEM images were also used to calculate fast fourier transforms for identification and labeling of d-spacings.
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, PHI 5000 VersaProbe III, AlKa), equipped with an Ar ion sputtering gun, was used to determine the oxidation state of the Cu and Bi elements in: as-deposited, post 10 min electrolyte immersion under open circuit, and after 10 min under bias at 1.0 VRHE samples. All measurements were performed at a pass energy of 55 eV for five cycles, and an X-ray beam spot size of 100 mm. The binding energy was corrected with reference to the adventitious carbon C 1s signal.

sections.heading: Electrolysis of CO2
sections.text:
A custom-built electrochemical cell was used for all ERC experiments. The electrochemical cell consisted of two cylindrical compartments separated by a proton exchange membrane (Nafion A117, 178 micron). The volume of the top and bottom compartments were 55 mL and 120 mL, respectively. All ERC experiments were controlled by using a potentiostat (Biologic SP-150) in a three-electrode setup with an Ag/AgCl reference electrode (Silver/ Silver Chloride, EAg/AgCl = + 0.6 VRHE at a constant pH of 6.8). All potentials were converted to reversible hydrogen electrode. The reference electrode was placed 0.5 cm away from the electrocatalyst, whereas the bottom compartment housed the Pt counter electrode. The electrolyte was comprised of KHCO3 (0.1 m; Alfa Aesar, 99.9 %) with a pH of 7.4. KHCO3 was purified by recrystallization and vacuum filtration before use. The electrolyte was saturated with high purity CO2 (99.99 %, Praxair) resulting in a pH of 6.8.
The procedure for each ERC experiment involved resistance (Ru) compensation, linear sweep voltammetry (LSV), re-compensation of resistance followed by ERC cycling. Resistance compensation was performed in addition to the automatic compensation of the potentiostat. LSVs were performed from OCP to 1.2 V versus RHE for electrochemical reduction of any oxide layers on the surface. All ERC experiments were performed at ambient conditions (25 8C, 1 atm) to a total charge of 50 C on a 3 cm2 electrode. After each ERC experiment, the gaseous products were manually syringed out and analyzed using a GC (Shimadzu gas chromatograph 2014) coupled with a thermal conductivity detector (TCD). The headspace produced at the end of an ERC experiment varied in volume based on the electrocatalyst and applied potential.

sections.heading: Product identification and measurement
sections.text:
GC was used to identify and measure the various gaseous reaction products. The instrument was equipped with a Restek RT-Qbond (30 m 8 mm) fused silica PLOT column and a 0.5 mL sample loop, in which the sample passes through three columns in series (Hayesep T 80/100 mesh 0.5 m 2.0 mm, Supelco 60/80 Mesh 5 molecular sieve 2.0 m 2.1 mm, and Hayesep Q 80/100 mesh 1.5 m

2.0 mm). High purity mixtures (Praxair) of H2, CO, CH4, and C2H4 were used to generate calibration graphs. At the end of an ERC experiment, 1 mL aliquots of gaseous products were injected into the sample loop with Ar as the carrier gas and identified by using a TCD. The sample chromatograms of these products are provided in Figures S2 and S3. Dimensionless Henry’s law constants[43] were used to calculate the amount of dissolved gas,[44] assuming vapor– liquid equilibrium.
Liquid products from the catholyte were determined by 1H NMR spectroscopy (10 % D2O, Varian 600 MHz). Solvent suppression of the H2O signal was necessary to increase the sensitivity of reaction products, especially those near the H2O peak. Trimethylamine-Noxide was selected as the standard (222 mm) to quantify the concentration of liquid products. Because of its singlet shape and chemical shift in the 1H NMR spectrum, use of trimethylamine-Noxide facilitated easier quantification of the liquid samples (Figure S4). Blank NMR spectra were acquired for every purified batch of electrolyte (KHCO3) to establish a baseline. Potassium formate was identified as the only measurable liquid product in these investigations.

sections.heading: Z. B. Hoffman, T. S. Gray, Y. Xu, Q. Lin,
High Selectivity Towards Formate Production by Electrochemical Reduction of Carbon Dioxide at
sections.text:
Copper–Bismuth Dendrites
Getting CO2 in format(e)ion : Cu–Bi bimetallic electrocatalysts for reduction of gaseous CO2 are synthesized by using electrodeposition. The efficiency, current density, and product selectivity of the catalysts are highly dependent on the composition and applied reduction potential. Optimized incorporation of Bi in Cu can achieve >90 % faradaic efficiency for formate production with a high product selectivity.
